 SNAP fight looms as ag leaders turn to farm bill in lame duck
 11/04/26 6:12 AM
 By Olivia M. Bridges and Kim Chipman 
 No Comments 
 Produce, which is covered by the USDA Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, is displayed for sale at a grocery store in Nashville, Tennessee. (AP photo/George Walker IV) 
 Congress has a limited window to push back the date for a first-ever SNAP cost-share requirement for states with high payment error rates. Without it, attempts to pass a bipartisan farm bill are dead.  
 States are bracing for millions of dollars in added costs while counties face a unique budgeting challenge. 
 New requirements in the OBBBA aim to motivate states to lower payment error rates, but a report finds doing so could come down to a matter of luck. 
 Agriculture leaders on Capitol Hill return to work next Monday under intense deadline pressure to reach a deal on Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program costs and pass a farm bill.
 A so-called lame duck session runs from Nov. 9, when the current Republican-led House and Senate reconvene, until early January, when a new two-year Congress convenes. 
 The total number of actual legislative working days during that period adds up to a little over four weeks. The time squeeze to move a new five-year farm bill following a string of delays comes as many crop farmers are worried about another year of soaring production costs and financial losses. 
 Senior Republicans and Democrats say passage of a farm bill this year is a top priority, but the measure has stalled in the Senate due to a partisan logjam over how long some states should get before having to start paying a portion of benefit costs from SNAP, the country's largest anti-hunger program. 
 Republicans say certain states need the required cost shift, which is part of the GOP's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), as incentive to lower their   SNAP payment error rates below 6%. Democrats say states on the hook to start paying benefit costs in 2027 need a delay of at least two years to prepare their budgets for the new costs. Senate Ag Chairman John Boozman, R-Ark., has offered a one-year postponement as the best deal Democrats will get.
 Meanwhile, New Jersey, one of 10 states in which SNAP is run at the county level, is in a special position come next Oct. 1.  The state's payment error rate, or PER, was cut in half from  14% in 2024  to just under  7% in 2025 . The drop means the state is now facing a lower cost-share rate. If New Jersey’s rate falls again in 2026, the state might not face a cost-share at all.  
 Yet the lower rate “doesn't make me feel better about the cost share," Larry Braasch, deputy division director in the New Jersey Division of Family Development, tells  Agri-Pulse. 
 Braasch, who has been dealing with the SNAP issue since the requirements became law through enactment of the OBBBA last year, has warned that the PER metric is “ fundamentally flawed .”  
 Democratic New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill sent letters   to her delegation last April, stating that PER is not an appropriate measuring tool, and that the cost-share provisions tied to it should be eliminated. Sherrill said the "PER cost shift" will cost the state another $98 million to $293 million each year, in addition to approximately $99 million in administrative SNAP costs that were increased under OBBBA and took force last month.  
 “The payment, the benefit cost-share, is predicated on the payment error rate for SNAP quality control, which is a fundamentally flawed metric,” Braasch said. “Even before this legislation started making its rounds, we were having conversations with the USDA to overturn their usage of it and what they were including in it and raised concerns about the statistical validity and reliability of the metric.” 
 Braasch said a big problem is a change from the Agriculture Department a few years ago that has led to much broader interpretations of "errors."  
 "So, instead of potentially just a thirty-dollar error, it might be a three-hundred-dollar error. Your entire allotment for the month, just because you were missing a single sheet of paper," he said. "That policy was specifically contrary to federal regulations, which say those are just administrative deficiencies."  
 Analysis  f rom the Hamilton Project found “there is no guarantee that good-faith efforts to improve program administration will be reflected in the form of a lower payment error rate.” SNAP quality control is conducted using a small subsample of cases and PER could come down to a matter of luck, according to the authors from the economic policy firm that's part of the Brookings Institution.  
 “Because the payment error rate statistic varies so widely and unpredictably from year to year, which states will have to make payments toward SNAP benefits, and what their contribution rate will be, varies by year,” the group says.  
 The paper concluded that “because random chance is a substantial factor in producing a state’s payment error rate in any single year, it is also true across time: The cost shift to states will fluctuate unpredictably and considerably from year to year based on random chance alone. We find that changes in payment error rates are not at all persistent across years and are more likely to reflect differences in a state’s luck of the draw in the quality control sample than changes in program administration.”

 New Jersey also faces an extra headache in its attempt to build a budget around the new financial obligations because of different calendars. The federal fiscal year begins Oct. 1, but the state’s fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30.  That's further complicated by the fact that the counties operate on the calendar year, making a predictable budget seem out of reach. 
 As far as this calendar year, states on Oct. 1 saw their federal match for SNAP administrative costs cut from 50% to 25%. In a little under a year, unless there's intervention from Congress, the SNAP benefit costs will kick in for the first time.

 SNAP participation across the nation fell by 5.5 million people, or 13%, between the law’s July 2025 enactment and July 2026, the latest month of available data, according to the  Center on Budget and Policy Priorities . Along with a longer runway for the SNAP costs, Democrats would like to undo the almost $200 billion in overall projected cuts to SNAP through 2034. 
 "These costs are so great that they could drive some states to end SNAP altogether," Katie Bergh, senior policy analyst on the food assistance team at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said last month. " This is already causing eligible families to lose SNAP. The amount a state will need to pay is determined by its error rate, the extent to which the state mistakenly over- or underpaid SNAP households. But delaying or denying SNAP to an eligible family doesn't count as an 'error.'" 
 Compromise ahead? 
 Sen. Amy Klobuchar, top Democrat on the Ag Committee who is expected to win her race to be Minnesota governor, is pushing for a two-year delay for some states, including her own. She's also stressed that finding a way forward to get a farm bill over the finish line this year is a top priority. 
 It's not clear, though, how Democrats overall might feel about advancing sweeping ag legislation, or any bills, during a lame duck session in which they still sit in the minority.
 The House passed its version of a farm bill in late April, but it doesn't deal with a SNAP delay and includes controversial provisions, such as language to nullify animal welfare rules like California's Proposition 12. Such language makes it a nonstarter in the Senate, where legislation typically must pass a 60-vote threshold to advance to the floor for full consideration. 
 Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a member of the ag panel, told reporters Tuesday morning that getting a five-year farm bill passed and signed into law can still happen this year, but it will take some compromise on SNAP. 
 "I hate to talk about compromising on getting fraud out of food stamps, but there may be some sort of compromise we'll have to do with the Democrats to get 60 votes to get the bill up," he said. 
 Negotiations among Senate and House agriculture committee staffers from both sides of the aisle began last month, though talks on SNAP aren't expected to take shape until after lawmakers return to Washington next week. 
 Republican aides, speaking on the condition of anonymity, speculate that Democratic members of Congress will be pressured by their state and local officials to take a one-year deal.
 Democrats, however, point out that the National Governors Association and eight other similar groups have pushed for a multi-year delay. States are scrambling to get a handle on the cost shifts, as are GOP-leaning counties  in places such as Minnesota, North Carolina and New York, which all administer SNAP at the county level.  
 In Clay County, a region of eastern Minnesota that’s been turning redder in recent election cycles, residents face a potential 4.1% increase in property taxes due to the SNAP program costs alone. 
 "Even in counties where the state will ultimately probably absorb the benefit cost share, we're worried about the overall fiscal pressure that comes from these really big costs on the benefit side coming down to the state, and the possibility always that the state could decide to push those down to counties," Emma Conover, associate legislative director for human services and education at the National Association of Counties, told Agri-Pulse .
 The farm bill would update ag programs that haven't been modernized since Congress last passed a full-year farm bill in 2018. Since then, key items covered in the legislation have been addressed through piecemeal measures, especially OBBBA and extensions amid ongoing partisan battles over issues like SNAP. Some ag policy watchers say the days of a traditional five-year, bipartisan farm bill may be over. 
 Peter Tabor, who co‑leads Holland & Knight’s Agriculture & Food Policy Team in Washington, told Agri-Pulse the outlook for getting a farm bill passed in the lame duck is "quite challenging." 
 "The SNAP issue is the gatekeeper,"  Tabor said.
